web strips of small width; giving a false twist to impart a certain strength to these strips;

1. SCOPE 

n 3AHAK J A 

1.1 This standard specifies the sequence of processes involved in the 
manufacturing of worsted, semi-worsted and woollen yarn. It Also tepict- 
fies the methods of test and permissible tolerances for various efcaractfcr4t- 
tics, packaging, marking, packing and sampling of yarn. - 1 ' ' ^ ■•■> '^ 

1.2 This standard does not specify the counts, breaking loj&frjfri&Jftlit jtf 
yarn. However, general information in respect of these is given in 
Appendix A. ' ; " " • ^

IS t9393-1979 

2. TERMINOLOGY 

2.0 For the purpose of this standard, the following definitions shall 
apply. 

2.1 Worsted Yarn — A yarn spun from wool fibres or blends which 
have been carded, gilled and combed followed by gilling before spinning. 
In the worsted system, an attempt is made to lay the fibres practically 
parallel along with the length of yarn which gives it a reasonably smooth 
surface. 

2.2 Semi-Worsted Yarn — A yarn spun from wool fibres or blends 
which have been carded and gilled before spinning. In the semi-worsted 
system, an attempt is made to lay the fibres somewhat parallel along the 
length of yarn, which gives it a slightly smooth surface. 

2.3 Woollen Yarn — A yarn spun from wool fibres or blends which have 
been carded only before spinning. In the woollen system, the carding 
process opens out and straightens the fibres which generally cross each 
other in every direction presenting a rough yarn surface* 

2.4 Metric Count — Number of 1 000 m hanks in one kilogram. 

2.5 Tex — Mass of 1 000 m of yarn in grams. 

3. SEQUENCE OF PROCESSES 

3.0 The sequence of processes for worsted, semi-worsted and woollen 
system of spinning of wool yarn is given in 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 respectively. 

3.1 Worsted System — The sequence of processes recommended for 
worsted system is given in Table 1. 

3.2 Semi-Worsted System — The sequence of processes recommended 
for semi-worsted system is given in Table 2. 

3.3 Woollen System — The sequence of processes recommended for 
woollen system is given in Table 3. 

4. CHARACTERISTICS 

4.1 The wool yarns shall be tested for the various characteristics by the 
methods given in Table 4. The permissible tolerances for these charac- 
teristics are also given in the table. 

5. PACKAGING 

5.1 The yarn shall be wound in hanks, cones or cheeses as agreed to 
between the buyer and the seller. Generally, the woollen yarn is wound 
in hank form while the worsted yarn is wound on cones and cheeses.

6. MARKING 

6.1 The yarn packages shall be marked with the following: 

a) Count of yarn; 

b) Description of yarn, namely, worsted, semi-worsted or woollen; 

c) Quality of raw wool/ wool top; 

d) Composition of yarn ( see IS : 1793-1973* ); 

e) Name of the manufacturer, initials or trade-mark, if any; and 

f) Month and year of manufacture.

6.1.1 The packages may also be marked with the ISI Certification 
Mark. 

Note — The use of the ISI Certification Mark is governed by the provisions of the 
Indian Standards Institution ( Certification Marks ) Act and the Rules and Regu- 
lations made thereunder. The ISI Mark on products covered by an Indian Standard 
conveys the assurance that they have been produced fo comply with the requirements 
of that standard under a well-defined system of inspection, testing and quality 
control which is devised and supervised by ISI and operated by the producer. ISI 
marked products are also continuously checked by ISI for conformity to that standard 
as a further safeguard. Details of conditions under which a licence for the use of 
the ISI Certification Mark may be granted to manufacturers or processors, may be 
obtained from the Indian Standards Institution.

8. SAMPLING AND CRITERIA FOR CONFORMITY 

8.1 Lot — The quantity of woollen, semi-worsted or worsted yarn of the 
same count and composition manufactured from the same quality of raw 
wool/wool top delivered to a buyer against a despatch note shall consti- 
tute a lot. 

8.2 The conformity of the lot to the requirements of the standard shall be 
determined on the basis of the test results obtained on the samples selec- 
ted from the lot. Unless otherwise agreed to between the buyer and the 
seller, the number of bales or cases to be, selected at random for drawing 
the sample packages shall be in accordance with the col 1 and 2 of 
Table 5. To ensure randomness of selection, methods given in IS : 4905- 
1968* shall be used. 

TABLE 5 NUMBER OF BALES OR GASES TO BE CHOSEN 
FROM A LOT 



Lot Size 
Bales or Gases

8.3 The number of packages to be selected from each bale or case 
selected according to 8.2 shall be five. The number of test specimens to 
be prepared from each package shall be such that at least 20 test speci- 
mens are available for carrying out the test for count, breaking load, 
twist and uniformity. The composite sample may be tested for extrac- 
table matter and commercial weight. 

8.4 Criteria for Conformity — The lot shall be considered conforming 
to the requirements of this standard if the following conditions are 
satisfied: 

a) The average count and twist of the test specimens lie between 
the relevant requirement; and 

b) The average breaking load value of the test specimen is not less 
than the specified or marked Value. 

c) All the test specimens subjected to the other tests satisfy the 
relevant requirements. 



♦Methods for random sampling.

A-2. BREAKING LOAD 

A-2.1 The lea breaking load value is always less than the sum of the 
breaking load values of the single threads comprising the lea. The lea 
and single thread breaking loads can be compared by means of ratio 'R f 
which is dependent on many factors like count, twist, etc. 

„ Average lea breaking load value 



n X Average single thread breaking load value 



*"!tat values are not exact equivalent* of woollen and worsted counts, these are the 
rationalised values recommended by the International Organization for Standardisation 
(ISO). 

10 



IS i 93*3 - 1979 

whtre n is number of threads in the lea and it can be determined by 
the following formula: 

2 X length of yarn in lea 
girth of lea 

A-2.2 The ratio of lea and single thread breaking load value for different 
types of yarn is given below: 

Type of Yarn Range of'R' Nominal Value 

Woollen 072-0-90 0'80 

Single worsted 0'40-0'82 0*65 

Two-fold worsted 67-0*94 0*80 

A-3. TWIST 

A-3.1 In general, the fibres in the yarn are twisted to the same angle 
throughout and hence the product of turns per metre and the square root 
of yarn in tex is kept constant. The formula, given below, thus helps in 
determining twist in yarn: 

_, Twist constant 
Turns per metre ■> 7-= 

Vtex 

A-3.2 Single Yarn — The twists in yarn depend upon the type of 
processing, quality of wool and the end uses. The twist constant provides 
a guide to the order of magnitude of twist generally accepted for some 
end uses. 

A-3.2. 1 Woollen Tarn — In general, the twist constant for different 
woollen yarns lay within the limits given below: 

Twist Designation Twist Constant 

Hard twist Greater than 5 400 

Medium hard 4 600-5 400 

Normal warp 3 800-4 600 

Normal weft 3 000-3 800 

Soft 2 200-3 000 

Very soft Less than 2 200 

A-3.2*2 Worsted Yarn — A general guidance can be had from the 
following formula: 

5 600 A" 
Turns per metre = - v^o" ' tex 

The value of ' K 9 depends to some extent on the performance for which 
the yarns are required. However, the yarn intended for use as a single 
yarn would generally be spun with higher twist than otherwise. 

A-3.3 Doable Yarn — Two-fold worsted yarns have the folding twist in 
the opposite direction to the spinning twist.

PUBLICATIONS OF INDIAN STANDARDS INSTITUTION 

INDIAN STANDARDS 

Over 10 000 Indian Standards covering various subjects have been 
Issued so far. Of these, the standards belonging to the Textile Group 
fall under the following categories; 

Aeronautical textiles Rayon fabrics, handloom 

Chemical test methods Ropes and cordages 

Colour fastness of textile Sampling of textiles, methods for 

materials Silk fabrics — handloom and 

Cotton fabrics— handloom, khadl, khadi 

and mill-made Sizing and finishing materials 

Dyestuffs Spinning machinery components 

Grading of fibres and yarns Terminology 

Grading of raw silk Textile floor coverings 

Hosiery Textile materials for fishing 

Jute — bags and fabrlci Textile mill accessories (other 

Jute mill accessories than jute mills) 

Narrow fabrics Twines 

National flag of India Weaving machinery components 

Nylon fabrics Wool fabrics — handloom, khadl, 

Packaging code and mill-made 

Physical test methods Yarn and similar structures 

Rayon fabrics Unclassified
